commands.desc: Create PR from commit info with label and reviewer
commands.tooltip: --fill pulls the title and body from your commit messages so you skip the editor prompts. --label attaches a label by name and --reviewer requests a review from a person or team by handle. Combine these flags to create fully-specified PRs in one shot instead of editing afterwards.

commands.desc: Create PR with explicit head and base branches
commands.tooltip: -H (head) names the branch holding your commits, overriding the current checkout. -B (base) names the branch your code merges into, so you can target main or a release branch without switching branches locally. Issue triage stays accurate because the PR is created against exactly the branch you name.

commands.desc: Create a draft PR with explicit title and body
commands.tooltip: --draft marks the pull request as a draft, signaling work-in-progress that cannot be merged yet. Drafts still run CI checks, so reviewers can comment early. Convert to a ready PR later with gh pr ready.

commands.desc: List recently merged pull requests
commands.tooltip: --state merged filters to PRs that have been merged, one of open, closed, merged, or all. --limit caps the result set at 50 rows, which keeps the output readable in a terminal. Useful for release-note mining or checking what shipped this sprint.

commands.desc: Search open PRs with a label via query
commands.tooltip: --search runs a GitHub search query with qualifiers like is:open, label:, and author: instead of using fixed filters. The query syntax mirrors the web UI's issue search box. Wrap the query in quotes so the shell does not split it.

commands.desc: List your own draft pull requests
commands.tooltip: --author @me is a shortcut that resolves to your authenticated login, while --draft keeps only work-in-progress PRs. Use --author with a teammate's handle to audit their open work. Combine with --state to flip between open, closed, and merged.

commands.desc: List PRs targeting main from a feature branch
commands.tooltip: --base filters by the branch the PR merges into and --head by the branch the PR comes from. Together they narrow the list to a single merge path, handy when multiple release branches are active. Values are branch names, not PR numbers.

commands.desc: List PRs as custom JSON-formatted lines
commands.tooltip: --json selects machine-readable fields and --jq applies a jq filter to reshape them, here printing number and title per line. The jq expression runs over the array of PR objects. This pattern feeds scripts, dashboards, and other tools without parsing gh's pretty table.

commands.desc: View PR metadata as JSON including changed files
commands.tooltip: --json returns the requested fields as a JSON object, and files expands to the list of paths the PR touches. Automate review checks by piping the output into jq. The field names match the GitHub API naming, so body is the PR description.

commands.desc: View a PR including its review comments
commands.tooltip: --comments appends the full comment thread to the PR view, mirroring the web page's conversation tab. Each comment shows author, timestamp, and body text. Leave the flag off for a compact summary of title, state, and checks.

commands.desc: Open a pull request in the browser
commands.tooltip: --web hands the PR URL to your default browser instead of printing a terminal summary. The browser tab lands directly on the PR conversation page. Use it when the terminal view cannot show the diff context you need.

commands.desc: Show the diff of a specific pull request
commands.tooltip: Prints the unified diff of all commits in the PR against its base branch, without checking anything out. Accepts a PR number, URL, or branch name. Add --name-only to list changed file paths instead of full diff content.

commands.desc: Check out a PR into a custom local branch
commands.tooltip: Fetches the PR's head branch and checks it out locally. --branch names the local branch, overriding the default of using the PR's head branch name, which avoids collisions when reviewing several PRs. Add --force to overwrite an existing local branch.

commands.desc: Squash-merge a PR and delete its branch
commands.tooltip: --squash collapses all commits into one before merging, keeping history tidy. --delete-branch removes both the remote and local branch after the merge completes. The merge only happens when required checks pass unless you add --auto or --admin.

commands.desc: Auto-merge a PR once checks pass
commands.tooltip: --rebase replays the PR commits onto the base branch without a merge commit. --auto schedules the merge so GitHub applies it automatically the moment required checks pass, ideal for unattended CI. Verify mergeable state with gh pr view before relying on it.

commands.desc: Force-merge a PR with admin privileges
commands.tooltip: --merge creates a standard merge commit while --admin uses repository administrator powers to merge even when required checks fail. Bypassing checks is risky and should be reserved for hotfixes where failure is understood. The merge is recorded with admin as the actor.

commands.desc: Convert a ready PR back to draft
commands.tooltip: gh pr ready flips a draft PR to ready-for-review, and --undo reverses the direction, returning a PR to draft status. Reverting to draft removes it from reviewers' queues. Useful when a PR regresses and needs more work before review.

commands.desc: Add a label to a pull request
commands.tooltip: --add-label attaches labels by name without opening the browser. Labels drive filtering and issue triage automation, so tagging needs-review routes the PR into review workflows. Multiple labels can be comma-separated in one flag value.

commands.desc: Remove a label from a pull request
commands.tooltip: --remove-label detaches the named label from the PR, for example clearing wip once the code is ready. Labels only match exact names, so confirm spelling with gh label list. Combine --add-label and --remove-label in one command to re-tag in a single call.

commands.desc: Close a PR with an explanatory comment
commands.tooltip: Closes the pull request without merging, and --comment leaves a closing note explaining why, such as pointing to a replacement PR. Closed PRs stay visible for history but drop out of open lists. Add --delete-branch to also clean up the head branch.

commands.desc: Comment on a PR with text from a file
commands.tooltip: --body-file reads the comment body from a file, handy for long, formatted review notes prepared in an editor. Use a dash (-) as the file to read the body from standard input. Existing comments stay untouched unless you pass --edit-last.

commands.desc: Approve a pull request
commands.tooltip: Submits an approving review for the PR, which counts toward required review checks. Approval signals the code is ready to merge from your perspective. Add --body to include review notes alongside the approval.

commands.desc: Request changes on a PR with a reason
commands.tooltip: --request-changes submits a review that blocks merging until the author responds, and --body explains what must change. This is the polite way to reject a PR while leaving actionable feedback. The PR stays open but shows changes-requested status.

commands.desc: Leave an inline-style review comment
commands.tooltip: --comment submits a general review comment without approving or blocking, distinct from --approve and --request-changes. It is the neutral review type for observations that do not gate the merge. Pair with --body for the message text.

commands.desc: Show CI check status for a PR
commands.tooltip: Lists every status check, workflow run, and review requirement attached to the PR with its state. Required checks are flagged so you see what blocks merging. Add --watch to poll until checks finish, or --fail-fast to exit on the first failure.

commands.desc: Watch PR checks until they complete
commands.tooltip: --watch polls check status repeatedly and streams updates as runs finish, like following a build to completion. The command exits when every check settles, so scripts can gate on the result. Combine with --interval to tune how often it polls.

commands.desc: Lock a PR conversation
commands.tooltip: Locks the PR so only maintainers can comment, and --reason records why: off_topic, too_heated, resolved, or spam. Locking stops drive-by noise on settled discussions. Reverse it with gh pr unlock.

commands.desc: Unlock a PR conversation
commands.tooltip: Removes a previous conversation lock so everyone can comment again. Use it when a locked PR needs fresh maintainer or contributor input. Lock state is per-PR and independent of merge state.

commands.desc: Update a PR branch against its base
commands.tooltip: Merges or rebases the base branch into the PR's head branch so the diff is current. --rebase replays your commits on top of the base instead of creating a merge commit. Useful before merging when the base moved on and conflicts are trivial.

commands.desc: List issues assigned to you
commands.tooltip: --assignee @me resolves to your login and filters the list to issues you own. This is the go-to command for your personal work queue during issue triage. Pass a teammate's handle to see their load instead.

commands.desc: List bug issues in a milestone
commands.tooltip: Combines --label and --milestone filters so only issues tagged bug within milestone v2.0 appear. Milestones group issues toward a release, and labels categorize them. Useful for sprint scoping when planning what must ship.

commands.desc: Search open bug issues with a query
commands.tooltip: --search runs full issue search syntax, here matching open issues labeled bug. Search supports qualifiers label:, assignee:, milestone:, and sort:. --limit caps output at 30. Filtering this way beats stacking many --label flags.

commands.desc: Open the issue list in the browser
commands.tooltip: --web opens the repository's issue tracker in your default browser with the current filters applied. Useful when you need the full web UI for bulk operations or saved views. The terminal list remains the faster path for simple queries.

commands.desc: View an issue with its comment thread
commands.tooltip: Prints the issue title, body, state, labels, and --comments appends the full discussion. Each comment shows author and timestamp, mirroring the web conversation. Leave the flag off for a compact metadata summary.

commands.desc: View issue fields as JSON for scripting
commands.tooltip: --json emits only the requested fields so scripts can consume them, with labels and assignees as nested arrays. Pipe into jq to build custom reports. Field names follow the GitHub API, so title is the issue's summary line.

commands.desc: Add a triage label to an issue
commands.tooltip: --add-label attaches the triage label, marking the issue as processed during issue triage workflows. Labels organize issues without changing state. Use --remove-label to strip stale tags and --milestone to slot it into a release.

commands.desc: Self-assign an issue and clear its triage label
commands.tooltip: Combines --add-assignee @me with --remove-label needs-triage in one call, claiming the issue and signaling it is being worked. @me expands to your login. This two-step triage dance happens constantly, so batching it saves a round trip.

commands.desc: Close an issue with a resolution note
commands.tooltip: Closes the issue and --comment leaves a note, here pointing at the PR that fixed it. Closing without a comment loses context for future readers. Use --duplicate-of to fold it into another issue instead of closing standalone.

commands.desc: Close an issue as a duplicate
commands.tooltip: --duplicate-of 12 closes issue 5 and links it as a duplicate of issue 12, consolidating triage noise into one canonical thread. GitHub shows a banner pointing readers at the original. Prefer this over closing duplicates with no pointer.

commands.desc: Lock an issue conversation
commands.tooltip: Locks the issue so only maintainers can comment, with --reason spam recorded for audit. Locking is the standard response to off-topic or abusive threads during issue triage. Unlock with gh issue unlock once the situation resolves.

commands.desc: Unlock an issue conversation
commands.tooltip: Removes the conversation lock, letting everyone comment again. Locking is reversible, so restoring discussion is one command away. Lock state is independent of open or closed status.

commands.desc: Unpin an issue from the repo top
commands.tooltip: Removes an issue from the pinned list shown at the top of the issue tracker. Pinned issues stay prominent, so unpin once the milestone ships or the thread goes stale. The issue itself remains open and fully searchable.

commands.desc: Create a dev branch for an issue
commands.tooltip: Creates a local branch wired to issue 5 so commits reference it, and --name sets the branch name, defaulting to issue-5. Add --checkout to switch to the branch immediately. This keeps development tied to triage-tracked work items.

commands.desc: Replace your last comment on an issue
commands.tooltip: Posts a comment and --edit-last rewrites your most recent comment instead of appending, keeping threads tidy when details change. The body replaces the old text entirely. Use --delete-last to remove your previous comment instead.

commands.desc: List every workflow including disabled ones
commands.tooltip: Shows all workflow files in the repo; --all includes disabled and hidden workflows that the default view omits. Each row shows the workflow ID, name, and enabled state. Use the ID with gh workflow enable or disable to toggle without typing the filename.

commands.desc: Re-enable a disabled workflow by ID
commands.tooltip: Turns a disabled workflow back on so it runs on its triggers again. The numeric ID comes from gh workflow list --json id and is more stable than a renamed file. Disabled workflows show in gh workflow list --all with a disabled badge.

commands.desc: Disable a workflow by ID
commands.tooltip: Stops a workflow from triggering on pushes, schedules, or manual runs without deleting its file. The numeric ID avoids filename ambiguity after renames. Re-enable anytime with gh workflow enable.

commands.desc: Manually trigger a workflow on a branch
commands.tooltip: Dispatches a workflow_dispatch run of build.yml, and --ref selects the branch or tag the workflow runs against. Only workflows with a workflow_dispatch trigger accept manual runs. Use this to kick off builds without pushing a commit.

commands.desc: Trigger a workflow with an input value
commands.tooltip: -f passes an input to the workflow in key=value form, here env=prod, which the workflow reads via inputs.env. Inputs must be declared in the workflow's workflow_dispatch section. Repeat -f to pass several inputs, or --json for typed values.

commands.cmd: gh workflow run release.yml --ref v1.2.0 -f version=1.2.0
commands.desc: Trigger a release workflow on a tag with input
commands.tooltip: Combines --ref v1.2.0 to run against the tag with -f version=1.2.0 to feed the workflow the version string. Tag-triggered release pipelines often need the version echoed as an input. Confirm the workflow accepts the input before dispatching.

commands.desc: Print a workflow's YAML definition
commands.tooltip: Displays the workflow file content instead of its run history. --yaml renders the raw definition, useful for reviewing triggers, jobs, and steps before editing. Without the flag, gh shows recent runs of the workflow.

commands.desc: Open a workflow's page in the browser
commands.tooltip: --web opens the workflow's dashboard in the default browser, showing its run history and YAML. Useful when you want the visual run timeline and logs. Terminal users get the same recent runs from gh run list --workflow.

commands.desc: List runs of one workflow on one branch
commands.tooltip: Narrows run history to a single workflow file and branch, cutting through noise on busy repos. --workflow accepts a filename or ID, --branch a branch name. Add --status to filter further, e.g. failure, for quick triage.

commands.desc: List the most recent failed runs
commands.tooltip: --status failure filters to runs that ended in failure, and --limit 10 caps the list. This is the fastest way to find broken CI. Other status values include success, cancelled, in_progress, and timed_out.

commands.desc: Open a workflow run in the browser
commands.tooltip: --web opens the run's page in the default browser, where logs, jobs, and artifacts are fully interactive. Terminal log tailing still works via gh run view --log. Use the web view when you need to retry individual failed jobs by clicking.

commands.desc: View failed logs of one job in a run
commands.tooltip: --job 424242 targets a specific job inside the run, and --log-failed prints only the failed steps' logs. Job IDs come from gh run view 123 --json jobs. This isolates the failing step without wading through the whole run log.

commands.desc: Watch a run and exit with its status
commands.tooltip: Polls the run until it finishes, streaming progress. --exit-status makes the command exit nonzero if the run failed, so CI wrapper scripts can gate on the result. Without it, gh always exits zero after watching.

commands.desc: Rerun a single failed job
commands.tooltip: Re-executes one job of a run instead of the whole pipeline, saving time and compute when only that job failed. --job takes the job ID shown by gh run view. The rerun counts as a new attempt on the same run.

commands.desc: Download run artifacts matching a pattern
commands.tooltip: Downloads artifacts uploaded by the run's jobs into dist/, with --pattern filtering to files matching the glob. Artifacts are the files jobs upload for later use, such as build outputs. Without --pattern, every artifact of the run downloads.

commands.desc: List secrets scoped to an environment
commands.tooltip: Shows secrets configured for the production environment, separate from repository-level secrets. Environments are protected scopes where secrets override repo-level values. Omit --env to list repository secrets instead.

commands.desc: Set an environment-scoped secret
commands.tooltip: Creates or updates MY_SECRET inside the production environment, and --body supplies the value non-interactively for scripting. Environment secrets are visible only to jobs referencing that environment. Prefer this over repo-wide secrets for deployment credentials.

commands.cmd: gh secret set MY_SECRET --org myorg --visibility selected --repos myapp,myapp-api
commands.desc: Set an org secret for selected repositories
commands.tooltip: Creates an organization-level secret shared across repositories, with --visibility selected limiting it to the repos in --repos. Visibility choices are all, private, or selected. Org secrets ease rotation: update once, and every permitted repo sees the new value.

commands.desc: Delete an environment-scoped secret
commands.tooltip: Removes MY_SECRET from the production environment, breaking any workflow that references it, so confirm nothing depends on it first. --env scopes the deletion to that environment. Without --env, the repo-level secret is removed.

commands.desc: List variables for an environment
commands.tooltip: Shows plaintext variables, not secrets, configured for the production environment. Variables hold non-sensitive config like URLs or feature flags, while secrets hold values that must stay hidden. Omit --env to list repository variables.

commands.desc: Set an environment-scoped variable
commands.tooltip: Creates or updates MY_VAR for the production environment with the given plaintext value. Unlike secrets, variable values appear in plain in workflow logs when referenced. Environment variables override repo-level ones of the same name.

commands.cmd: gh variable set MY_VAR --org myorg --body 'value' --visibility selected --repos myapp
commands.desc: Set an org variable for selected repos
commands.tooltip: Creates an organization-level variable shared across repositories, with --visibility selected restricting it to the repos listed in --repos. Org variables centralize config like shared registry URLs. Values are stored as plaintext.

commands.desc: Delete an environment-scoped variable
commands.tooltip: Removes MY_VAR from the production environment, so any workflow reading it must supply a fallback or fail. --env targets the environment; without it the repo-level variable is deleted. Deleting is immediate and not recoverable via gh.

commands.desc: Create a release with auto-generated notes
commands.tooltip: Creates release v1.1.0 from the tag, and --generate-notes has GitHub draft the changelog from merged PRs and commits since the last release. --target pins the branch or SHA the release builds from. Edit the auto notes before publishing if they need polish.

commands.desc: Create a release with notes from a file
commands.tooltip: --title sets the release heading while --notes-file reads the body from CHANGELOG.md, keeping long release notes out of the command line. The file's content becomes the release description verbatim. This is the standard flow for hand-maintained changelogs.

commands.desc: Create a prerelease with artifacts attached
commands.tooltip: --prerelease marks the release as a release candidate so it is not flagged as the latest stable version, and the file arguments upload dist/*.tar.gz as assets. Prereleases stay clearly labeled in the releases list. Promote later with gh release edit --latest.

commands.desc: Create a draft release with generated notes
commands.tooltip: --draft creates the release without publishing it, visible only to maintainers, and --generate-notes prefills the body from merged PRs. Drafts let you review notes and assets before going public. Publish by editing --draft=false or via the web UI.

commands.desc: Upload an asset replacing same-name files
commands.tooltip: Attaches dist/app.zip to release v1.1.0, and --clobber overwrites any existing asset with the same filename instead of erroring. Re-uploading without --clobber fails if the name is taken. Assets are the downloadable binaries, archives, and checksums of a release.

commands.desc: Download release assets matching a glob
commands.tooltip: Downloads matching assets from release v1.1.0 into /tmp/releases. --pattern filters files by glob, handy when a release carries several formats. Without --dir, files land in the current directory. Add --clobber to overwrite existing files.

commands.desc: Download the source archive of a release
commands.tooltip: --archive tar.gz fetches the source code snapshot GitHub generates for the release, not an uploaded asset. Choose zip or tar.gz. This is the canonical way to get the exact code of a tagged version for auditing or vendoring.

commands.desc: View release metadata as JSON
commands.tooltip: --json returns release fields such as tagName, assets, and publishedAt for scripts. assets expands to an array of attached files with sizes and download counts. Pair with --jq to shape the output into reports or CI checks.

commands.desc: Open a release page in the browser
commands.tooltip: --web opens the release's public page, where assets, notes, and download buttons are rendered. Use it to double-check what users will see. The terminal view shows the same metadata as text.

commands.desc: List the 20 most recent releases
commands.tooltip: Shows recent releases with tag, title, and date. --limit caps the list at 20 rows for terminal readability. Add --exclude-drafts and --exclude-pre-releases to show only stable, published releases.

commands.desc: List only published stable releases
commands.tooltip: Filters out draft and prerelease entries so only fully published releases remain, capped at 10. Useful for changelogs and release dashboards where unstable versions would pollute the list. Compare with --json to script the filtered set.

commands.desc: Mark a release as latest and retitle it
commands.tooltip: --latest promotes the release to be the newest stable release GitHub recommends, useful after promoting a release candidate, and --title rewrites its heading. The body and assets stay untouched. Demoting is done with --latest=false.

commands.desc: Delete a release and its tag
commands.tooltip: Permanently removes release v1.1.0; --cleanup-tag also deletes the git tag it points to, and --yes skips the confirmation prompt. Deleting a release breaks download links and, with --cleanup-tag, the tag, so verify nothing references it. This action cannot be undone.

commands.desc: List your container packages via API
commands.tooltip: Queries the REST endpoint for packages owned by your account, filtering to container images, and --jq prints each package name. Packages are images and libraries published under your user or org. Listing via gh api unlocks filters the gh CLI has no native command for.

commands.desc: List versions of a container package
commands.tooltip: Hits the package versions endpoint and prints each version ID, the handle used to delete or inspect individual image versions. Container images accumulate versions on every push. Combine with DELETE on the same endpoint to prune old images.

commands.desc: Create a private repo with README and clone it
commands.tooltip: Creates myorg/webapp under your organization, --private sets visibility, --add-readme seeds the repository with a README, and --clone checks it out locally afterwards. One command replaces several web clicks. Swap --private for --internal or --public as needed.

commands.desc: Create a repo from a template
commands.tooltip: --template owner/express-starter scaffolds the new repository from the template's files and history, and --public sets visibility. Template repos copy starter code, CI, and docs so every new project starts consistent. Omit --clone to skip the local checkout.

commands.desc: List archived repos in an organization
commands.tooltip: Lists repositories owned by myorg, --archived filters to archived ones, and --limit caps output at 50. Archived repos are read-only and useful to audit for cleanup or reference. Drop --archived or add --no-archived to flip the filter.

commands.desc: List repos tagged with a topic
commands.tooltip: --topic hacktoberfest filters repositories by their topic tags, which are community-applied keywords on the repo page. --limit 30 keeps the table short. Combine with --language to narrow by stack. Great for finding repos participating in events.

commands.desc: View repo metadata as JSON
commands.tooltip: Fetches repository fields such as name, description, and stargazerCount as JSON for scripting. stargazerCount is the star total, a rough popularity signal. Add --jq to format or filter the fields further.

commands.cmd: gh repo edit owner/repo --description 'CLI tool' --homepage https://example.com
commands.desc: Edit repo description and homepage
commands.tooltip: Updates the repository's description and homepage URL in one call, both of which appear on the repo's public page. The --repo flag can target any repo you can write to. Other editable fields include topics, visibility, and merge settings.

commands.desc: Auto-delete head branches on merge
commands.tooltip: Turns on delete-branch-on-merge for the current repository so merged PR branches are cleaned up automatically. Set to false to disable. This is a repo-level setting that keeps the branch list tidy with zero manual work.

commands.desc: Sync a fork from its upstream
commands.tooltip: Pulls commits from --source upstream/repo into owner/repo, keeping a fork current with the project it derives from. Without --source, gh syncs from the fork's configured parent. Add --force to discard local diverging commits.

commands.desc: Fork a repo under a different name
commands.tooltip: Creates a fork of owner/repo and --fork-name names it myapp-copy, useful when the original name is taken or you want a distinct copy. The fork lands in your account by default. Add --clone to check it out locally right away.

commands.desc: Fork only the default branch
commands.tooltip: Creates a fork containing just the repository's default branch instead of every branch, saving storage and clone time. Ideal when you only need the mainline for contributions. Branches can be fetched from the original later if needed.

commands.desc: Choose the default repo for gh commands
commands.tooltip: Prompts you to pick which repository subsequent gh commands should assume when none is specified. The choice is saved per-directory, so each project can pin its own repo. View the current selection with --view or clear it with --unset.

commands.desc: Shallow-clone a repo via git passthrough
commands.tooltip: Everything after the -- is forwarded to git clone, here --depth 1 for a shallow checkout with no history. Pass any git flag this way, such as --branch or --filter. Shallow clones are much faster for large repositories.

commands.desc: Rename a repository
commands.tooltip: Renames owner/repo to myapp-v2; -R targets a specific repo and --yes skips the confirmation prompt. Renaming changes the URL, breaking existing clones and bookmarks, so update remotes afterwards with git remote set-url. The old URL redirects for a while.

commands.desc: Create a gist from stdin and open it
commands.tooltip: The dash positional reads gist content from standard input, so you can pipe output from any command into it. -w opens the newly created gist in the browser. By default gists are secret; add --public to share them.

commands.desc: Create a public gist with a description
commands.tooltip: Uploads script.py as a gist, --public makes it visible to anyone with the URL, and --desc attaches a short description. Gists are lightweight code snippets with their own git history. Secret gists remain private but are not encrypted.

commands.desc: Add a file to an existing gist
commands.tooltip: --add notes.md appends a new file to gist 1234, letting a gist grow from a snippet into a small project. The file content is read from your working directory. Remove files again with --remove.

commands.desc: Remove a file from a gist
commands.tooltip: --remove old.txt deletes that file from gist 1234, updating the gist's content set without recreating it. Gist edits are recorded in the gist's revision history. Pair --add and --remove in one command to restructure a gist in a single step.

commands.desc: List only your public gists
commands.tooltip: Shows your public gists, with --public filtering out secret ones. The list shows each gist's description, filename, and visibility. Add --limit to cap rows, or --secret to list only private gists.

commands.desc: List your secret gists
commands.tooltip: --secret filters to gists only you can see, capped at 50 rows. Secret gists are private-by-URL but not encrypted, so avoid sensitive data. The default listing mixes both visibilities.

commands.desc: View one file inside a gist
commands.tooltip: Prints the contents of script.py from gist 1234. --files selects specific files when a gist holds several, avoiding a long concatenated dump. Without it, all files print in sequence.

commands.desc: Create a codespace for a repo and branch
commands.tooltip: Provisions a new codespace, a cloud-hosted dev environment, for owner/repo on branch main. Codespaces run in a container configured by devcontainer.json. The machine type defaults sensibly; tune it with --machine.

commands.cmd: gh codespace create --repo owner/repo --branch main --machine standardLinux32gb
commands.desc: Create a codespace with a specific machine
commands.tooltip: Adds --machine standardLinux32gb to request a 32 GB RAM instance, matching the machine names shown by gh codespace list or the web UI. Bigger machines cost more, so pick by workload. The codespace is ready to connect via ssh, code, or the web.

commands.desc: SSH into a running codespace
commands.tooltip: -c names the codespace to connect to, as shown by gh codespace list. This drops you into a shell inside the container, identical to SSHing to a VM. Codespace names look like yourname-project-random; omit -c to pick interactively.

commands.desc: List forwarded ports of a codespace
commands.tooltip: Shows which ports inside the codespace are forwarded to your local machine and their visibility. Forwarding lets you reach dev servers running in the container via localhost. Change visibility with gh codespace ports visibility.

commands.desc: Expose a codespace port publicly
commands.tooltip: Sets port 3000's visibility to public so anyone with the URL can reach the forwarded service, not just you. Choices are public, private, and org. Public exposure is for demos; keep development ports private.

commands.desc: Delete a codespace
commands.tooltip: Permanently removes the named codespace, including its container filesystem and any uncommitted work inside it, so commit or push first. Deleted codespaces cannot be restored. Add --force to skip the confirmation prompt.

commands.desc: Stop a running codespace
commands.tooltip: Shuts down the codespace's container, stopping compute charges while preserving its filesystem. Start it again on next connection. -c targets a specific codespace; without it you pick from a list.

commands.desc: Stream a codespace's logs
commands.tooltip: Prints the codespace's container logs, and --follow tails them live like tail -f. Useful when a devcontainer fails to build or a service crashes at startup. The logs come from the codespace's lifecycle and application output.

commands.desc: Fully rebuild a codespace container
commands.tooltip: Rebuilds the codespace's dev container from its definition, and --full skips cached layers for a clean build. Use it when devcontainer.json changes or the environment is corrupted. A rebuild recreates the container but keeps your files.

commands.desc: View codespace status as JSON
commands.tooltip: --json returns machine-readable fields like state, which is Available, Shutdown, or Building, and idleTimeoutMinutes, the idle limit before auto-stop. Pair with --jq for monitoring scripts. State tells you whether the codespace is ready to connect.

commands.desc: List codespaces as JSON
commands.tooltip: Lists your codespaces with --json fields name, repository, and state for scripting. Field names come from the codespace API, so repository is the owning repo. Add --repo to filter by project or --limit to cap rows.

commands.desc: Install a gh extension, forcing upgrade
commands.tooltip: Installs the gh-copilot extension from the github org, and --force upgrades an existing install to the latest release instead of erroring. Extensions add new gh subcommands, here gh copilot for AI assistance. Pin a version with --pin to freeze it.

commands.desc: Upgrade a single gh extension
commands.tooltip: Updates the gh-copilot extension to its newest released version. --force upgrades even when the local version matches, useful after a manual edit or to escape a stuck state. Use --all to update every installed extension at once.

commands.desc: Remove a gh extension
commands.tooltip: Uninstalls the gh-copilot extension, removing its subcommand from gh. Extensions are user-local, so removal affects only your account. Reinstall anytime with gh extension install github/gh-copilot.

commands.desc: Scaffold a new gh extension
commands.tooltip: Generates the directory layout and starter files for a gh extension named my-extension. Extensions are standalone scripts or Go binaries that add gh subcommands. Add --precompiled to scaffold a Go-based extension instead of a script.

commands.desc: Print your GitHub username via API
commands.tooltip: GETs the authenticated user endpoint and --jq extracts the login field. The leading slash is optional in gh api paths. This is a quick identity check that also confirms your token works.

commands.desc: Fetch issue numbers with a page size
commands.tooltip: Requests the issues endpoint with per_page=100 to grab more rows per call, and --jq prints each issue number. Pagination caps REST responses at 30 by default, so raising per_page reduces round trips. Use --paginate to walk all pages automatically.

commands.desc: Close an issue via the REST API
commands.tooltip: -X PATCH switches the HTTP method, and -f sends state=closed as a form parameter, closing issue 5 without gh issue close. REST endpoints map one-to-one with GitHub's API documentation. The -f flag adds string parameters; -F infers typed values.

commands.cmd: gh api graphql -f query='query($owner:String!,$repo:String!){ repository(owner:$owner,name:$repo){ stargazerCount } }' -f owner=cli -f repo=cli
commands.desc: Query stargazer count via GraphQL with variables
commands.tooltip: Runs a GraphQL query where every -f field except query becomes a GraphQL variable, here binding $owner and $repo. GraphQL lets you request exactly the fields you need in one round trip. Variables make queries reusable across repos.

commands.desc: Get the latest release tag via API
commands.tooltip: Hits the latest-release endpoint and prints the tag name, handy for CI that must fetch the newest version. The endpoint ignores prereleases. Compare with gh release list --limit 1 for tag plus metadata.

commands.desc: Fetch a workflow run record via API
commands.tooltip: Returns the full JSON record of run 123: status, conclusion, head SHA, and event. Scripts use this to gate deploys on CI results. It is the REST equivalent of gh run view minus the pretty formatting.

commands.desc: List all workflows via API, following pages
commands.tooltip: --paginate automatically walks every page of results until exhausted, since REST caps at 30 items per page. The workflows endpoint returns each workflow's id, name, and state. Combine with --jq to extract the fields you need from the full list.

commands.desc: Dispatch a workflow run via the REST API
commands.tooltip: POSTs a workflow_dispatch event for build.yml on ref main, the API equivalent of gh workflow run. The workflow must declare a workflow_dispatch trigger. Pass inputs as extra -f fields if the workflow defines them.

commands.desc: Delete all Actions caches for a repo
commands.tooltip: Wipes every Actions cache entry in the repository, freeing storage but forcing cold builds until caches rebuild. This is destructive and irreversible, so run it only when cache bloat is a real problem. --silent suppresses the success response body.

commands.desc: Show your API rate limit usage
commands.tooltip: Queries the rate-limit endpoint and prints remaining and total requests for your token, e.g. 4800/5000. REST APIs throttle unauthenticated calls hard, so staying under the limit matters for scripts. Reset time lives in the .rate.reset field.

commands.cmd: gh api -X POST repos/owner/repo/issues/5/comments -f body='Fixed in #10'
commands.desc: Comment on an issue via the REST API
commands.tooltip: POSTs a comment to issue 5 with the body field, the API form of gh issue comment. Use this when automation, not a human, must post context like CI results. The comment appears in the issue thread like any other.

commands.desc: Star a repository via the API
commands.tooltip: PUTs the current user's star on owner/repo, the API equivalent of clicking the star button. --silent drops the empty success body. Unstar with -X DELETE on the same endpoint. Starring is a lightweight signal of interest or approval.

commands.desc: Fetch a file's raw contents via API
commands.tooltip: GETs the README through the contents endpoint, and the -H Accept header for the raw media type returns the file bytes instead of base64 JSON. Contents endpoints also list directory trees. This is a scriptable way to pull a file without cloning.

commands.desc: Print the auth token for a host
commands.tooltip: Outputs the OAuth token gh uses for github.com, which scripts and other tools can reuse. The token grants the same permissions as your gh login, so treat it like a password. --hostname selects among hosts when you have several accounts.

commands.desc: Add scopes to the current token
commands.tooltip: -s requests additional scopes, here repo for full repository access and workflow for updating Actions files. Scopes are the permission grants attached to your token. Refresh interactively confirms via the browser and merges the new scopes in.

commands.desc: Log in via browser with SSH git protocol
commands.tooltip: Authenticates gh for github.com, --git-protocol ssh makes git operations use SSH URLs, and --web completes the flow in the browser. The web flow avoids pasting tokens into the terminal. Log out anytime with gh auth logout.

commands.desc: Show auth status including the token
commands.tooltip: Prints which accounts and hosts gh is authenticated as, with --show-token also revealing the token itself. The token is a live credential, so this output can be captured by shell history or logs. Prefer plain gh auth status unless a tool truly needs the token.

commands.desc: Log out of a specific host
commands.tooltip: Revokes the gh credential for github.com, so gh commands requiring auth start failing until you log in again. --hostname targets one host when multiple are configured. Logging out does not delete your git credentials unless they were gh-managed.

commands.desc: Set git protocol to SSH
commands.tooltip: Writes git_protocol ssh into gh's config so git clone and push use SSH URLs, which need an SSH key set up on GitHub. The other value is https. Your existing remotes are not rewritten by this setting.

commands.desc: Read the configured git protocol
commands.tooltip: Prints the current git_protocol value, either ssh or https. Config lookups check host-specific overrides first, then global settings. Useful in scripts that must branch on the transport gh will use.

commands.cmd: gh config set git_protocol https -h github.com
commands.desc: Override git protocol for one host
commands.tooltip: -h scopes the setting to github.com, so that host uses HTTPS while others keep their own protocol. Host-scoped overrides beat global config for that host. This is how you mix transports across accounts or Enterprise servers.

commands.desc: Show config for a specific host
commands.tooltip: Lists resolved gh settings, with -h github.com filtering to that host's overrides. The output shows keys like git_protocol, editor, and prompt. Use it to debug why a command behaves differently on one host.

commands.desc: Set the pager for long gh output
commands.tooltip: Configures the pager gh pipes long output through, here less with -F quit-if-one-screen, -R raw color, and -X no-clear flags. A sensible pager keeps tables readable. Set it to cat to disable paging entirely.

commands.desc: Create a short alias for a gh command
commands.tooltip: Defines prd as a word that expands to gh pr view, so gh prd 123 shows a PR. Aliases can embed flags, like 'pr list --state merged'. They live in gh's config and work exactly like built-in commands.

commands.cmd: gh alias set --shell prd 'gh pr view "$1"'
commands.desc: Create a shell-based alias with arguments
commands.tooltip: --shell marks the expansion as a shell expression, evaluated through a shell interpreter, so $1 captures the argument after the alias. Here gh prd 123 runs gh pr view 123. Shell aliases unlock pipes, loops, and argument manipulation plain aliases cannot do.

commands.cmd: gh alias set merged 'pr list --state merged --limit 20'
commands.desc: Alias a multi-flag pr list query
commands.tooltip: Bundles a full command with flags into the single word merged, so gh merged prints your last 20 merged PRs. Aliases that encode routine queries save keystrokes and enforce consistent flags. Overwrite an existing alias by adding --clobber.

commands.desc: Export all aliases to a YAML file
commands.tooltip: Dumps every alias as YAML to standard output, redirected here into aliases.yml. The file round-trips with gh alias import, making aliases portable across machines. Export before wiping a config or setting up a new workstation.

commands.desc: Install bash completion for gh
commands.tooltip: -s bash generates the bash completion script, redirected into ~/.bash_completion so your shell sources it at startup. Tab-completion then fills subcommands, flags, and repo names. Re-run after upgrading gh if completions go stale.

commands.desc: Install zsh completion for gh
commands.tooltip: Writes the zsh completion script into the standard site-functions directory, which zsh loads automatically. The file must be named _gh for zsh to associate it with the gh command. Requires a zsh version of 5.7 or later.

commands.desc: Install fish completion for gh
commands.tooltip: Generates the fish completion script into fish's completions directory, where it loads on the next shell start. Fish autoloads completion files by command name, so gh.fish is picked up automatically. Works identically for powershell with -s powershell.

commands.cmd: gh copilot suggest -t gh 'create a release from the latest tag'
commands.desc: Ask Copilot to suggest a gh command
commands.tooltip: gh copilot suggests a command for the natural-language request, and -t gh constrains the answer to gh commands rather than shell or git. It returns the command plus an explanation, ready to copy. Requires the gh-copilot extension and a Copilot subscription.

commands.desc: Ask Copilot to explain a git command
commands.tooltip: gh copilot explains what the given command does, flag by flag, in plain language. Useful for decoding unfamiliar git invocations. Add -t git to pin the target context when the command is ambiguous.
